correctness.rationale: For every rank-three 3x7 binary generator matrix, the rank-deficiency event after t samples is exactly a seven-plane minus twice seven-line plus eight-zero-subspace Möbius sum. Its geometric series yields the rational expression in the proof. There are exactly C(14,7)=3432 possible column multiplicity profiles on the eight vectors; rank closure filters exactly 2696 full-rank profiles. The supplied standard-library verifier checks all 2696 with both the subspace expression and the independent information-set subset-rank expression. It separately directly enumerates all 8^7=2097152 ordered matrices, matching multinomial profile weights and 1984248 full-rank matrices. Each binary [7,3] code has 168 row bases; the exact 42-row histogram and moments follow by exact integer and Fraction arithmetic. The 42 second-tier profiles and one equivalence orbit are checked by exhaustive comparison and GL3(F2) action. This is an exhaustive finite proof only at these exact parameters; no infinite extrapolation or independent audit is claimed.

originality.rationale: Bertuzzo, Ravagnani and Yaakobi explicitly gave the numeric 47/12 simplex mean and second-best lower bound 17/4 for binary [7,3] in arXiv:2507.20639 Example 1, so neither number or its 1/3 gap is claimed new. Kong et al. arXiv:2610.02931 and Gross et al. arXiv:2610.07370 prove simplex optimality generally; the latter derives a random-code ensemble mean. The new finite statement identifies all 42 possible coverage expectations and their exact counts among the 11811 labeled linear codes, their nonzero ensemble variance and all 630 second-level codes in one orbit. The inspected prior source sections do not state or logically specialize directly to this full evaluated distribution without an additional exhaustive classification. Unindexed or unpublished computation remains a specific residual risk.

value.rationale: The binary [7,3] simplex is the first nontrivial projective-plane benchmark explicitly considered in the founding paper and later optimality results. Knowing only the best and second numeric expectations, or even the random-code mean, does not determine the spread across the entire set of 11811 distinct code designs. The exact 42-atom histogram and ensemble variance give a complete comparison for uniform random choices of codes; the exact 630-code second tier and unique geometric orbit explain which near-best designs exist. A natural full finite classification with reproducible integer proof, not an arbitrary numerical slice, is valuable as a canonical small-field benchmark and robustness description. Its usefulness is limited to error-free uniform sampling and finite [7,3] codes; no coding-rate claim is made.
